title: Lighter Than Air: France and England, 1783–1785
places: Above Paris, from La Muette to the Butte-aux-Cailles
Garden of La Muette, near Passy
His carriage near the statue of Louis XV
North Mymms and Standon Green End, Hertfordshire
Dover Castle to the forest of Guînes
Champ de Mars and the Tuileries, Paris
Passy, on the western edge of Paris, a short walk from La Muette
London, and his Lincolnshire estate during the summer recess
Réveillon's garden, La Muette, Versailles, Boulogne-sur-Mer
In the gallery of the Montgolfier balloon over Paris
intro: In the eighteen months between June 1783 and January 1785 people went from watching a paper globe rise over a market town in the Vivarais to crossing the sea by air. The idea, the first trials and a kind of mastery all fall inside two years, and they happened in public, before kings, crowds of tens of thousands, and some of the most careful letter-writers of the age. Two methods raced each other. The Montgolfier brothers, papermakers from Annonay, filled their envelopes with smoke and heated air; the physicist Jacques Charles and the Robert brothers used the 'inflammable air' (hydrogen) that chemists had only lately learned to make. Within weeks of each other, Paris saw an unmanned hydrogen globe vanish into cloud, a sheep, a duck and a cockerel go up before Louis XVI, men lifted on a rope in a wallpaper maker's garden, and finally two men carried freely across the city. The honest record here is mostly letters and published accounts rather than diaries. Benjamin Franklin, American minister at Passy, watched several of the ascents and wrote long letters about them to Joseph Banks at the Royal Society; Banks's replies show London moving from wonder to caution. Faujas de Saint-Fond turned the experiments into a book almost as they happened. The aeronauts themselves — d'Arlandes, Charles, Lunardi, Jeffries — wrote accounts for publication, which makes them vivid and self-interested at once. Some of the people who mattered most left almost nothing. The villagers of Gonesse, who attacked the first hydrogen globe as a monster, appear only through the government's notice telling the public not to be afraid. James Sadler, the Oxford pastry cook who became the first English aeronaut, wrote nothing; what survives is what reporters set down. Pilâtre de Rozier, the first man to fly, is seen through procès-verbaux, newspapers and his companions. The chapter crosses to England in 1784, when Lunardi, Sadler and Blanchard made the first ascents there and Horace Walpole mocked the craze, and ends with the Channel crossing of Blanchard and Jeffries in January 1785. Its coda is sober: in June 1785 Pilâtre de Rozier and Pierre Romain were killed trying to cross the other way, the first deaths in the air.

title: Steam on the Water: the Hudson and the Atlantic, 1807–1838
eyes: Moses Rogers (master) and the log of the Savannah
Anonymous passenger of the Great Western
places: Dock near the State Prison, North River, New York
Paulus Hook ferry, New York, to Albany
Port Glasgow to the Broomielaw, Glasgow
Great Western Railway directors' meeting, Bristol/London
Sandy Hook to the Battery, New York
New York Lower Bay and the Narrows
Aboard the Sirius, off the Battery
On the Hudson between New York and Albany, 17–21 August 1807
Helensburgh and Glasgow, on the Clyde
Bristol and aboard the Great Western on the Thames
intro: Steam came to water before it came to land, and it came first as a river boat. In August 1807 Robert Fulton took a long, narrow, noisy boat with an English engine up the Hudson from New York to Albany, 150 miles in 32 hours of running, and back in 30. Sloops on the same river could take a day or a week depending on the wind. Within three weeks the boat was carrying paying passengers on a timetable. The record of that week is mostly letters, not diaries. Fulton wrote to his partner Robert R. Livingston, to the newspapers and to his friend Joel Barlow; Peter Augustus Jay, sailing up the same river on his wedding journey, went aboard and wrote to his father that the thing was fast but costly and cramped. In Scotland Henry Bell's Comet opened a passenger service on the Clyde in 1812, recorded mainly in advertisements and in Bell's own later letters claiming priority. The ocean was a different problem: not speed but coal. The Savannah crossed from Georgia to Liverpool in 1819 with an engine and folding paddle wheels, but her own log shows she sailed most of the way and ran out of fuel off Ireland. When Bristol men set out to build a true Atlantic steamer in the 1830s, the lecturer Dionysius Lardner argued that no steamer could prudently run much more than about 2,080 miles without coaling. He did not say steam could never cross the ocean, as later legend has it; he said the arithmetic of the ships then proposed would not work. Brunel's answer was size: a ship's capacity grows faster than its resistance, so a large enough hull could carry its own coal. His Great Western, launched at Bristol in July 1837, nearly burned on the Thames eight days before her maiden voyage, and Brunel himself was badly hurt. Meanwhile a rival London company chartered the small Irish Sea packet Sirius to get to New York first. The Sirius left Cork on 4 April 1838 and anchored off the Battery late on 22 April; the Great Western left Bristol on 8 April and came up the next afternoon with nearly 200 tons of coal to spare. Who was 'first' depends on the measure: the Savannah first to cross with steam, the Canadian Royal William of 1833 often cited for a largely steam crossing, the Sirius first into New York under continuous steam in 1838, the Great Western first built for the service and first to prove it could be run as a business. The eyes here include an engineer, rival captains, a promoter, an expert who doubted, an anonymous passenger, a city diarist and a newspaper editor. The crews and stokers who did the work barely appear in the record beyond complaints of long shifts and the stokers who rowed ashore in panic during the fire.

title: Rainhill and the Opening Day, 1829–1830
places: Liverpool to the Sankey viaduct and back
On the line between Liverpool and Manchester
In the state carriage of the Northumbrian's train
In the Duke's carriage at Parkside
In one of the trains following the Duke's
In one of the following trains, Liverpool to Manchester and back
intro: In the spring of 1829 the Liverpool & Manchester Railway had a line almost built and no settled way to move trains along it. Two respected engineers, James Walker and John Rastrick, had toured the colliery railways of the North-East and reported that ropes wound by fixed engines in engine-houses along the route would be cheaper than locomotives. The directors chose not to decide on paper. They offered £500 for a locomotive that could meet set conditions, and in October 1829 five machines came to a level stretch at Rainhill to try for it. The trials are recorded unusually well, because they were a test with rules. Rastrick, one of three judges, kept a notebook of weights and timings; the Mechanics' Magazine and the Liverpool papers reported every day; the Stephensons and their rival Timothy Hackworth left letters. The figures do not always agree, and the press did not pick the winner: the light London engine Novelty, built by John Braithwaite and John Ericsson, was the crowd's favourite. Rocket, built by Robert Stephenson with a many-tubed boiler suggested by the company's treasurer Henry Booth, was the only engine to finish. Between the trials and the opening come the first passengers' verdicts. Thomas Creevey, a sardonic Whig, rode in November 1829 and found the speed frightening. The actress Fanny Kemble rode the footplate beside George Stephenson in August 1830 and found it thrilling. Her letter, written the next day and printed in 1878, is the best-known early description of a locomotive ride. On 15 September 1830 the line opened with the Prime Minister, the Duke of Wellington, as guest of honour. At the Parkside water stop William Huskisson, MP for Liverpool and a long-time supporter of the railway, stepped down to greet the Duke, was struck by Rocket on the adjoining line and died at Eccles that evening. The eyes here saw it from different distances: Harriet Arbuthnot from the Duke's carriage, Charles Babbage from a train that simply stopped, Edward Stanley and Kemble in the procession, and Greville and Creevey through letters and gossip days later. The procession went on to Manchester to a hostile reception from crowds who saw the Duke as the enemy of reform, and returned to Liverpool late at night. Most of this record is letters, notebooks, newspapers and printed accounts rather than diaries, and the form tags say so. Babbage's memoir was written thirty-four years later, and Mrs Arbuthnot's journal was published only in 1950, so it is paraphrased without quotation. The men who dug the cuttings and laid the line across Chat Moss, and the enginemen who drove the trains (Joseph Locke was on Rocket's footplate at Parkside), left almost no words of their own. They appear in company records and in other people's accounts, not as eyes.

title: Joining the Oceans and the Continent, 1869
eyes: Chinese workers of the Central Pacific (payrolls and press)
San Francisco, Sacramento and Salt Lake newspapers
Friedrich Wilhelm, Crown Prince of Prussia (later Emperor Frederick III)
Egyptian fellahin of the corvée (company, state and later records)
The Spectator and the London press
places: Sierra summit tunnels, Cisco to Truckee
Aboard the Prussian flotilla, Port Said to Ismailia
Omaha and the UP line across Wyoming and Utah
UP end-of-track camps at Echo and Weber, Utah
San Francisco, Sacramento, Salt Lake City
intro: In 1869 two pieces of the world's transport map were joined six months apart. On 10 May at Promontory Summit, Utah, the Central Pacific building east from Sacramento met the Union Pacific building west from Omaha, and a telegraph operator sent one word across the country. On 17 November the Empress Eugénie's yacht L'Aigle led some forty ships into the Suez Canal, and three days later the procession reached the Red Sea. A continent had been crossed by rail and two oceans by a ditch through the desert. The honest record of both is mostly not diaries. It is company letters and payrolls, chief engineers' reports, dated photographs, speeches as the newspapers printed them, a crown prince's privately printed travel diary, a painter's notebook, and a poet's verse letter written a year later. Where that is the form of the source, the entries say so. Several eyes are institutions or collective records rather than single diarists. Both works were built by labour that left almost no words of its own. The Central Pacific's workforce was overwhelmingly Chinese, perhaps ten thousand or more men at its height; they appear in payrolls as 'China Men', in newspapers as numbers, and at Promontory only at the edges of the photographs, though a Chinese gang laid the last rail. The Suez Canal's first channel was dug by Egyptian peasants conscripted under the corvée until Napoleon III's arbitration ended the system in 1864; how many died is contested, from the 120,000 of Nasser's 1956 speech to historians who say no archive supports that figure. Both are traced here through the records that kept them, and the gaps are stated. The ledger of trials runs from concession to opening: the strike of 1867, the ten miles and 56 feet laid by hand on 28 April 1869, the disputed mileages of the final spike, the joining of the seas in August, and a later, unconfirmed story of a British survey ship slipping ahead of the Empress in the dark. Distances, depths and dates are given as the record gives them, with rival figures shown side by side. Read together, the two openings show the same pattern from different sides of the world: owners and engineers who spoke of commerce with Asia and India, photographers and painters who composed the official image, a press that counted miles and dividends, and workers who appear only when someone else wrote them down.

title: The Road: Bicycles and Motorcars, 1888–1908
eyes: Croydon inquest on Bridget Driscoll (coroner Percy Morrison)
Prince Scipione Borghese, Prince of Sulmona
places: Jackson Park, Chicago, to Evanston and back
In the Itala from Peking to Paris
Mannheim (filed with the Imperial Patent Office, Berlin)
Reigate, Surrey, at Lady Henry Somerset's home
Dolphin Terrace, Crystal Palace grounds, London
Mannheim, then on the road to Pforzheim and back
intro: In August 1888 a woman of thirty-nine took her husband's three-wheeled motor carriage out of a Mannheim workshop before dawn, put her two teenage sons aboard, and drove roughly a hundred kilometres to her mother's house in Pforzheim. That same summer a Belfast veterinary surgeon was patenting an air-filled tyre he had first fitted to his small son's tricycle. Twenty years later, cars were being driven from Peking to Paris and from New York to Paris, with newspapers paying for the petrol and selling the story by telegraph. This chapter follows the ordinary road through those two decades, when the bicycle and the motorcar arrived together and the open highway became a place for trials, wagers, races and the first deaths. The record is uneven, and the chapter says so. Bertha Benz left no diary; her drive is known from what her husband wrote in his 1925 memoir and from later family retellings, so even the day is disputed. Dunlop told his own story late in life. Frances Willard wrote a short, cheerful book about learning to ride at fifty-three. Annie Londonderry's round-the-world ride survives mostly in newspaper interviews she gave as she went, and she was a gifted and unreliable self-promoter. The early races are known from the newspapers that organised them, whose figures (distances, times, prize decisions) are the closest thing to a test log, and from participants' later books such as H. O. Duncan's. The motor age's first deaths reached the record through inquests. When Bridget Driscoll was struck by a demonstration car in the grounds of the Crystal Palace in August 1896, the coroner's court heard six hours of evidence about speed, a restricted engine, and a driver who may or may not have rung his bell. The jury's finding, and the coroner's hope that it would not happen again, are reported here as the court recorded them. The Peking–Paris race of 1907 is the best-documented journey in the chapter, because it was made for the newspapers. Luigi Barzini rode in Prince Scipione Borghese's Itala and wired dispatches to the Corriere della Sera and the Daily Telegraph, then turned them into a book that was in English within months. Jean du Taillis did the same for Le Matin from the Spyker of Charles Godard, a penniless adventurer who borrowed the car and was arrested before the finish. Ettore Guizzardi, the Itala's mechanic, who did much of the driving, left no writing of his own; he survives in Barzini's pages. The New York–Paris race of 1908 closes the chapter, with George Schuster's Thomas Flyer arriving after more than five months. Read together, these eyes show the road being re-invented from below: a housewife testing an invention, a vet testing a tyre, a temperance leader and a working mother turning the bicycle into a public argument about women's freedom, editors staging races to sell papers, and an inquest jury trying to decide who was responsible when a machine killed a pedestrian.

title: Kitty Hawk, 1896–1903
eyes: The Virginian-Pilot (Harry P. Moore and the Norfolk desk)
places: Houseboat on the Potomac near Chopawamsic Island, Quantico, Virginia
Small boat on the Potomac near Quantico
Albemarle Sound, aboard Israel Perry's schooner; Kitty Hawk
Kill Devil Hills, four miles south of Kitty Hawk
Train from North Carolina to Dayton
The bicycle shop, 1127 West Third Street, Dayton
Mouth of the Anacostia, below Washington Barracks
Level ground below Kill Devil Hill
Beside the launching rail, Kill Devil Hills
Washington (Smithsonian Contributions to Knowledge, vol. 27, no. 3)
Kitty Hawk and Kill Devil Hills camps
Dayton, Ohio, and on church travels
Gollenberg hill near Stölln, Rhinow hills, Brandenburg
On the houseboat and a small boat on the Potomac near Quantico, 6 May 1896
Aboard the Great Aerodrome on the houseboat at Widewater, Virginia
On the sand beside the launching rail, 17 December 1903
Huffman Prairie, near Dayton, after driving from Medina
intro: In the summer of 1896 two men stood at opposite ends of the idea of human flight. On 6 May Samuel Pierpont Langley, Secretary of the Smithsonian Institution, watched a steam-driven model with no one aboard circle above the Potomac for more than half a mile while Alexander Graham Bell photographed it. Three months later Otto Lilienthal, who had made some two thousand glides from hills near Berlin, stalled in a gust, fell and died the next day. One line of work trusted power and stability; the other trusted the pilot's skill. In Dayton, Ohio, two bicycle makers read about Lilienthal's death, and within three years Wilbur Wright was writing to the Smithsonian for whatever it had printed on flight. This chapter follows that idea from letters to a sand camp to a field of corn stubble. The honest record is unusually rich: Wilbur's and Orville's diaries and notebooks, their weekly letters home, their father Bishop Milton Wright's terse daily diary in Dayton, sister Katharine's letters, the long correspondence with the Chicago engineer Octave Chanute, and the camp diary kept for Chanute in 1901 by Edward Huffaker, who was there mostly to fight mosquitoes and doubt the Wrights' front elevator. Much of it is letters and logs rather than diaries in the narrow sense, and it is tagged that way. Against the Wrights stands Langley's well-funded programme, seen through Langley's own account and through Charles Manly, the young engineer who rode the full-size Great Aerodrome off a houseboat into the Potomac twice, on 7 October and 8 December 1903, and wrote the record down for the Smithsonian's memoir of 1911. Nine days after the second plunge, on a cold Thursday morning on the Outer Banks, Orville Wright flew 120 feet in 12 seconds, and Wilbur, at noon, 852 feet in 59 seconds. The witnesses on the beach were few and local: the Kitty Hawk postmaster Bill Tate, whose letter of 1900 invited the Wrights to the Banks, and the surfmen of the Kill Devil Hills Life-Saving Station, among them John T. Daniels, who squeezed the bulb of a borrowed camera and later told the story all his life. The news then went wrong almost at once: a Norfolk reporter, working from a leaked telegram, invented a three-mile flight, and editors in Dayton shrugged. Only a beekeeping editor from Medina, Ohio, Amos Root, printed an accurate eyewitness account, of the first circle flown at Huffman Prairie in September 1904. The ledger of trials sets their measured figures side by side, and it includes the long quarrel afterward: in 1914 a modified Langley Aerodrome hopped off Lake Keuka at Hammondsport and the Smithsonian called the original machine capable of flight; Orville disputed it for nearly thirty years until the Institution retracted the claim in 1942. Both positions are given as positions, with their evidence.

title: Across the Channel and the Atlantic, 1909–1927
places: Rockaway, New York, to off Chatham
San Diego to St Louis to New York
intro: In July 1909 the English Channel, about twenty-two miles of grey water between Calais and Dover, was the obvious test for the aeroplane. The Daily Mail had offered £1,000 for the first crossing. Hubert Latham went first and came down in the sea. Six days later Louis Blériot, limping from a burned foot, crossed in roughly thirty-seven minutes in a small monoplane with no compass, and landed hard in a meadow under Dover Castle while a French reporter waved a tricolour to guide him in. Within three years the Channel was a route rather than a feat. When Harriet Quimby flew it in April 1912, the first woman to do so, she flew by compass through fog, and the news was buried under the loss of the Titanic. The next obstacle was the Atlantic. The Daily Mail raised its offer to £10,000 in 1913, and the First World War paused the attempt and supplied the means: long-range bombers, flying boats, rigid airships and men trained to fly them. In May and June 1919 the ocean was crossed three ways within seven weeks. The US Navy sent three Curtiss flying boats in stages via Newfoundland and the Azores, with warships stationed along the route. Only NC-4, under Albert Read, got through. John Alcock and Arthur Whitten Brown then flew nonstop from Newfoundland to an Irish bog in a converted Vickers Vimy bomber, through fog, sleet and a spin that took them nearly down to the waves. In July the airship R34 crossed from Scotland to Long Island and flew home again. In New York, a French-born hotelier, Raymond Orteig, offered $25,000 for the next step, a nonstop flight between New York and Paris. Nobody claimed Orteig's prize for eight years. When the contest finally turned fierce in 1926–27, it cost lives: René Fonck's overloaded Sikorsky crashed on take-off, killing two of the crew, and Noel Davis and Stanton Wooster were killed in a test flight. Charles Nungesser and François Coli left Paris for New York on 8 May 1927 and disappeared. Twelve days later Charles Lindbergh, alone in the Spirit of St. Louis, left a muddy Roosevelt Field and landed at Le Bourget on the night of 21 May, where a crowd overran the field. Two weeks after that, Clarence Chamberlin flew Charles Levine, the first transatlantic aeroplane passenger, to a field near Eisleben in Germany. The record is mostly not diaries. It is logs, official reports, telegrams, newspaper dispatches, prize letters and accounts the flyers published within months. Brown's book (1920) and Lindbergh's "We" (1927) were written while the events were fresh. Lindbergh's much longer The Spirit of St. Louis (1953) is a later reconstruction and is not used here. Mechanics, escort crews, ground handlers and the fishermen who met these flyers mostly survive only as names, or as crowds, in the flyers' own accounts.

title: Airships, 1900–1937
eyes: South Trimble Jr. (US Department of Commerce accident board)
places: Aboard the Graf Zeppelin, Lakehurst to Lakehurst
Avenue des Champs-Élysées at rue Washington, Paris
Aboard R34, over the North Atlantic
Lakehurst, New Jersey, and over New York
Aboard the Graf Zeppelin, over the Atlantic
Kasumigaura Naval Air Station, near Tokyo
intro: For thirty-seven years the airship was the way to fly far. Count Ferdinand von Zeppelin's first rigid ship lifted off Lake Constance on 2 July 1900 and stayed up for about twenty minutes. A year later a young Brazilian in Paris, Alberto Santos-Dumont, steered a small cigar-shaped balloon around the Eiffel Tower and back against the clock. By 1929 the Graf Zeppelin had circled the globe with paying passengers, a meteorologist, foreign naval officers and a woman reporter aboard. By 1936 the Hindenburg ran a timetable across the North Atlantic. Then on 6 May 1937 it burned at Lakehurst in about half a minute, and the age ended. This chapter follows that arc from idea to trial to mastery to loss. Zeppelin's diary entry of 1874 sketches the first idea. Santos-Dumont's own book, My Airships (1904), records his trials and falls in Paris. Brigadier-General Edward Maitland's published log of R34 follows the first east-to-west flight across the Atlantic by air, in July 1919, with a stowaway aboard. Hearst's correspondents Lady Grace Drummond-Hay and Karl von Wiegand radioed dispatches from the Graf Zeppelin over Siberia and the Pacific. A Philadelphia lawyer's private diary of a 1936 Hindenburg crossing shows the ship as its passengers knew it: the catwalk, the smoking room, the slow circle over home. The losses are told plainly. LZ 4 burned at Echterdingen in 1908, and a national collection rebuilt Zeppelin's enterprise. R101 struck a hillside near Beauvais in October 1930, and 48 of the 54 people aboard died. The Hindenburg fire killed 36. Two formal inquiries, Sir John Simon's into R101 and the paired American and German inquiries into the Hindenburg, are given here as findings, with the points where they differed. The wartime Zeppelin raids on Britain, Belgium and France from 1915 appear only briefly. Volume I's First World War chapter carries them. Much of this record is not diary in the strict sense. It is published logs, wire dispatches, company flight logs, official reports, a radio recording and memoirs written decades later: Hugo Eckener's and Nevil Shute's, the latter from 1954. Each eye's form is tagged honestly. Twentieth-century texts are given as paraphrase only. Short quotations appear only from English texts published before 1929, from United States government reports, or as one world-famous phrase. Read side by side, the eyes show the same craft from the inside and from below. There is the commander working out lift against heat and rain, the reporter asking for breakfast on the first morning, the engineer who built the rival ship, the inquiry judge weighing gasbags and down-currents, the passenger at the dining-salon window, and the radio man on the field.

title: Rockets, 1926–1957
eyes: Charles Greeley Abbot and the Smithsonian Institution
The New York Times (editorial page and news desk)
Wernher Magnus Maximilian Freiherr von Braun
TASS (Telegraph Agency of the Soviet Union) and Pravda
J. Allen Hynek and the Moonwatch network
places: Clark University and his Aunt Effie Ward's farm at Auburn, Massachusetts
Times building, West 43rd Street, New York
intro: On a snowy March afternoon in 1926 a small frame of pipes on a Massachusetts farm let go a rocket that flew for two and a half seconds. Thirty-one years later a 58-centimetre sphere was beeping round the Earth every 96 minutes, heard by radio amateurs, the BBC and a Moscow newsroom alike. This chapter follows rocketry across those three decades, from the first liquid-fuel hop to orbit. The record is uneven. Robert Goddard kept a daily diary and notebooks, but they reached print only in 1970, edited by his widow Esther and G. Edward Pendray. In Germany and the Soviet Union, the amateur rocket societies left test records and minutes, but most first-person accounts are later memoirs by Willy Ley, Rudolf Nebel and Wernher von Braun, each with reasons to shade the story. Sergei Korolev's letters became public only after his death. Most entries are therefore digests of letters, test records, institutional publications and press reports, and each eye's form tag says which. Three lines run side by side. Goddard worked almost alone, first with Smithsonian grants and then, through Charles Lindbergh, with Guggenheim money in the New Mexico desert. In Germany, Hermann Oberth's 1923 book set off a public enthusiasm: the Society for Space Travel and its Berlin rocketport, a film premiere, and young volunteers. In Moscow, Friedrich Tsander and Korolev ran GIRD. By the end of 1933 both amateur movements had been absorbed by their armies. The German Army line produced the A4, the V-2: the first large liquid-fuel rocket and a weapon. It was built from 1943 in tunnels in the Harz by concentration-camp prisoners. Historians estimate that more of them died in the Mittelbau-Dora camps than were killed by the missile in London, Antwerp and elsewhere. After the war its engineers and hardware were divided between the victors. Under Operation Paperclip von Braun's team came to Texas while captured V-2s flew from White Sands, and Soviet engineers under Korolev rebuilt German work alongside their own. The chapter ends on 4 and 5 October 1957, seen from several places: Korolev's midnight call from the steppe, TASS's understated announcement, and the volunteer Moonwatch network in Cambridge, caught unready and sorting real sightings from false ones. The New York Times, which in 1920 had told Goddard a rocket could not work in a vacuum, frames the chapter. It printed its correction in July 1969, as Apollo 11 flew to the Moon.

title: Faster Than Sound and the Jet Age, 1947–1969
eyes: The aviation and weekly press: Flight, Aviation Week, The Spectator
British Overseas Airways Corporation (BOAC) and its crews
The Comet courts of inquiry (India 1953; Lord Cohen, London 1954–55)
Juan Terry Trippe and Pan American World Airways
Andrei Nikolayevich Tupolev and the Tupolev design bureau
places: Over Muroc Dry Lake, about 42,000–45,000 ft
Tyrrhenian Sea, about 70 miles south of Naples
Toulouse, at the roll-out of Concorde 001
intro: On 14 October 1947 a small orange rocket aircraft fell away from a B-29 over the Mojave Desert, fired its engine, and went faster than sound. The pilot's report runs to a few typed lines about drop speed, cylinders and a meter that ran off its scale. The engineers' data, the injury he hid, and the fact that no one was supposed to know at all came out in other papers. Twenty-two years later, airliners designed to cruise at twice that speed were flying from Toulouse, Filton and Moscow. This chapter follows the path between them. Very little of it is diary. The honest record of the early jet age is flight reports, test records, conference papers, company announcements, parliamentary debates, inquiry reports and the weekly aviation press, with memoirs written decades later by the test pilots. The form tags say which is which. The one true diarist is Tony Benn, the minister responsible for Concorde, whose diary shows the doubt inside the enthusiasm. Because nearly all of this was published after 1928, the entries are digests; the only quotation is a line from Yeager's US-government flight report. The middle of the chapter is the de Havilland Comet. It made the first jet airliner flight in 1949 and the first jet passenger service in 1952, and then three BOAC-owned Comets were lost with everyone aboard within a year: near Calcutta in May 1953, off Elba in January 1954 and south of Naples in April 1954. Those deaths are stated plainly. The investigation that followed is one of the great pieces of engineering detective work. The Navy recovered wreckage from the sea, and at Farnborough Arnold Hall's team pressurised a whole fuselage in a water tank until it cracked. Lord Cohen's court then traced the Elba failure to fatigue at the cut-out for an aerial window in the cabin roof. Hansard records the same months from Westminster: grounding, sabotage rumours and the decision to make the cure a national project. While the Comet was grounded, others moved. Boeing's Dash 80 flew in 1954 and Tex Johnston rolled it over a Seattle hydroplane race in 1955. Juan Trippe ordered Pan Am's jets that October. The Soviet Tu-104, built from a bomber, landed in London in 1956 and began the first uninterrupted jet airline service across Siberia. In October 1958 a rebuilt Comet 4 and Pan Am's 707 opened transatlantic jet service three weeks apart. The coda is the supersonic transport: the Tu-144 on the last day of 1968, Concorde 001 under André Turcat in March 1969, and 002 under Brian Trubshaw at Filton in April, with Benn watching. Ordinary passengers are hard to find in this record. The 36 who flew to Johannesburg in 1952 left no traced diaries, and the 1958 Pan Am travellers are known mainly through recollections gathered sixty years later. They appear here through the airlines' and newspapers' counts, and the gap is left visible.

title: The Bullet Train: Japan, 1957–1964
eyes: International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (World Bank)
places: East portal of the Shin-Tanna tunnel, near Atami
Tokyo bureau and the test trains
JNR headquarters, Tokyo, at the opening ceremony
intro: On a spring evening in 1957 four researchers from the national railways' research institute stood on the stage of a concert hall in Ginza and told an audience of more than five hundred that a train could run from Tokyo to Osaka in three hours. The fastest existing express took seven and a half. Seven years and four months later, on 1 October 1964, two trains named Hikari left Tokyo and Shin-Osaka at six in the morning and met their timetable of four hours; a year after that the time was three hours ten minutes. This chapter is built from records rather than diaries. The engineers left lectures, technical papers and, decades later, memoirs and interviews; the chief engineer Shima Hideo's own account was written in the 1990s and is flagged as such. The railway corporation left chronologies, timetables and construction records; the World Bank left a loan agreement; the government and the Imperial Household left published ceremonial records; and foreign readers met the line through Time magazine and the wire services. The passengers of opening day barely appear by name in the accessible record: the reports say only that the first trains were full. Two threads run through the story. One is the engineers. Several of RTRI's key researchers, including Miki Tadanao and Matsudaira Tadashi, had designed and tested military aircraft for the Navy; Kawanabe Hajime came from the Army. Barred from aviation after 1945, they turned wind tunnels and vibration theory onto trains, and historians still debate how far their outsiders' science, and how far the railways' own engineers, made the difference. The other thread is money. JNR president Sogō Shinji pushed the line through on an estimate of ¥194.8 billion, framed it as an addition to the old Tōkaidō Line, and took an $80 million World Bank loan that bound the state to finish it. The real cost was about ¥380 billion. In May 1963 Sogō was not reappointed and Shima resigned with him; neither was invited to the opening. Accounts differ on how much the overrun, the deliberately modest estimate, or the Mikawashima accident of 1962 counted against him, and those differences are reported here as positions. The line opened nine days before the Tokyo Olympics, the first railway built for regular service above 200 km/h. Laying the engineers' plans, the institution's figures, the lender's paperwork and the foreign press side by side shows how an idea announced to a hall of railway enthusiasts became a timetable.
